# Verdant Complete Battle Guide

This is the campaign-order guide to every reachable trainer definition. Optional fights are kept in their earliest chapter; rematches and postgame challenges are separate. Levels use the active strict cap plus the listed offset.

Reachable battle definitions: **810**  
Internal unused definitions excluded from the walkthrough: **44**

# Opening rival battle

## 001. May — Route 103

**Required Branch · Single · Cap 14 · Brutal 75/100 · Uniqueness 41/100**

**Theme:** residual control

The rival always fields the type-counter starter from the same regional trio the player chose. It is level 15, one above the strict cap, with perfect IVs, a Life Orb, its universal Pledge STAB, Return, Toxic, and Protect. The encounter supports all 21 starters across Generations 1-7 through one native counterpart rule, while May and Brendan remain mechanically identical. It introduces Verdant's preparation freedom without pretending the player already owns a full team.

**How it behaves:** The normal foe-aware viability AI chooses among offense, Toxic, and Protect. No opening is forced and no hidden lock-and-key sequence is required.

**Why it is hard:** 1 fully authored Pokémon, average BST 310.0, average cap offset +1.0, ace offset +1, and 100% held-item coverage.

**How unique it is:** Closest unrelated roster: Brendan (100% species overlap). Its species appear across an average of 2.0 unrelated trainer families.

**Counterplay:** There is no single required solution. The player can use any legal coverage or status plan their chosen starter supports, or lean on Focus Sash, Eviolite, Leftovers, Life Orb, or a Choice item from Oldale. Protect, setup, Counter or Mirror Coat, Endeavor, speed control, and direct offense are all viable on different starters.

**Manual closure:** Battle 1 is a dangerous but open-ended first preparation check: the rival's exact counterpart matches the player's chosen generation, its +1 level and competitive item establish Verdant's 7.5 floor, and multiple legal plans can still win without a starter-specific lock.

# Stone Badge

## 007. Calvin — Route 102

**Optional · Double · Cap 14 · Extreme 82/100 · Uniqueness 92/100**

**Theme:** Fake Out tempo + Sash Endeavor lure + active speed control

Zorua leads beside Friend Guard Jigglypuff while Illusion makes it appear to be the Mew held in the final slot. Icy Wind and Helping Hand turn the false Mew into immediate pressure; Focus Sash Smeargle then creates a redirection or Fake Out window for the real Mew to use Nasty Plot and clean. This is Calvin's playground illusion team: the first apparent Mew is a local Zorua, the second is real, and Smeargle plus Jigglypuff make the deception function as a complete four-Pokémon plan. No later encounter will reuse this false-ace structure.

**How it behaves:** Calvin uses normal foe-aware doubles scoring plus partner support, speed-control preference, and smart switching. No move or turn is forced; the sets are deliberately legible to the general AI.

**Why it is hard:** 4 fully authored Pokémon, average BST 367.5, average cap offset +0.5, ace offset +1, and 100% held-item coverage.

**How unique it is:** Closest unrelated roster: Amy & Liv (14% species overlap). Its species appear across an average of 1.5 unrelated trainer families.

**Counterplay:** This team has several answers rather than one key. Spread attacks expose Illusion and bypass Follow Me, Taunt shuts down Jigglypuff or Smeargle, priority finishes a Sash-broken Smeargle, and early Bug, Ghost, and Dark options pressure Mew. The player can also double-target the support slot, contest speed with their own Icy Wind or Electroweb, or overwhelm the frail Zorua lead.

**Manual closure:** Battle 2 is the first full-team doubles exam. It is difficult because the player must identify the false Mew, manage active speed and partner support, and preserve an answer for a level-15 Nasty Plot Mew—not because the battle demands one preselected counter.

## 008. Rick — Route 102

**Optional · Single · Cap 14 · Extreme 82/100 · Uniqueness 86/100**

**Theme:** Bug pressure + web offense

Focus Sash Water Bubble Dewpider establishes Sticky Web while threatening real special coverage. Choice Band Anorith immediately punishes the Fire and Flying attacks invited by the Bug theme, Eviolite No Guard Karrablast is the only setup threat, and level-16 Life Orb Larvesta closes through recoil-limited physical pressure and U-turn rather than a mature Quiver Dance sweep. This is Verdant's juvenile Bug Web lesson: all four species are first-stage, Anorith and Karrablast appear on no other current trainer, Dewpider appears only in mutually exclusive later rival branches, and Larvesta's other uses are substantially later. The mature Leavanny/Scizor/Heracross/Frosmoth version is preserved for a cap-55 Bug specialist.

**How it behaves:** Rick remains an intentional singles pacing fight. First-turn setup preference makes Sticky Web or Karrablast's Swords Dance worth considering, while smart switching and normal foe-aware scoring preserve attacks, Choice locking, recovery, and pivots. No move or opening is forced.

**Why it is hard:** 4 fully authored Pokémon, average BST 324.8, average cap offset +1.0, ace offset +2, and 100% held-item coverage.

**How unique it is:** Closest unrelated roster: Bernie (20% species overlap). Its species appear across an average of 1.5 unrelated trainer families.

**Counterplay:** Taunt, multihit attacks, or immediate pressure can deny Web; Flying and Levitate Pokémon ignore it, and legal removal clears it. Wingull, Shinx, Blitzle, Rotom, Bonsly, Rock coverage, priority, and faster Choice users are already available. Intimidate, burns, and physical walls constrain the three backliners, while Water and Rock pressure force Larvesta to spend recoil or recovery turns. No one counter is required.

**Manual closure:** Battle 3 is 10/10 because it proves unevolved Pokémon can support a real competitive hazard plan. Web feeds three distinct physical tempos, but the team has one Sash, one setup slot, exploitable shared weaknesses, recoil, a Choice lock, and several independent forms of counterplay.

## 009. Tiana — Route 102

**Optional · Double · Cap 14 · Extreme 85/100 · Uniqueness 89/100**

**Theme:** Ice pressure + snow engine

Focus Sash Snow Warning Amaura and Eviolite Slush Rush Alolan Sandshrew lead with Aurora Veil, accurate Blizzard, fast Ice and Steel pressure, and Brick Break utility. Choice Band Thick Fat Swinub adds Ice Shard priority, Rock Slide spread damage, and Superpower, while level-16 Expert Belt Slush Rush Arctozolt is the single-stage Bolt Beak ace. This is Verdant's first full weather battle and its juvenile fossil snow lesson. Amaura and Alolan Sandshrew appear on no other current trainer, Swinub's only other use is a much later level-one gimmick, and no Battles 1-4 species repeats. The mature Ninetales-A/Froslass/Mamoswine shell is preserved for cap-70 Route 133 trainer Linda.

**How it behaves:** Tiana uses foe-aware smart switching plus field-control and first-turn setup preferences. Snow is automatic; Aurora Veil receives a contextual bonus without being forced, and the now-irrelevant generic speed-control profile is removed because no team member uses an active speed-control move.

**Why it is hard:** 4 fully authored Pokémon, average BST 354.2, average cap offset +1.0, ace offset +2, and 100% held-item coverage.

**How unique it is:** Closest unrelated roster: Linda (14% species overlap). Its species appear across an average of 1.8 unrelated trainer families.

**Counterplay:** Remove or replace snow, Taunt or double-target Sash Amaura before Veil, break Veil, or use Wide Guard against Blizzard and Rock Slide. Fire, Fighting, Rock, Steel, Ground, and Water coverage hit different members; Flying and Levitate avoid Ground coverage, priority and Trick Room bypass Slush Rush, and Intimidate or burns contain all three physical attackers. Protect punishes Bolt Beak timing, and the team has no second setup mode once Veil is denied.

**Manual closure:** Battle 5 is 10/10 because three young Pokémon and one true fossil create a complete snow puzzle without premature evolutions. Weather, Veil, two distinct Slush Rush attackers, priority, spread damage, and Bolt Beak make it severe, while every dependency has several independent answers.

## 010. Allen — Route 102

**Optional · Double · Cap 14 · Extreme 82/100 · Uniqueness 88/100**

**Theme:** Fake Out tempo + active speed control + priority pressure

Light Ball Lightning Rod Pikachu and Toxic Orb Guts Taillow lead with Fake Out, Electroweb speed control, priority, immediate damage, and protection from Electric targeting. Eviolite Dry Skin Paras and Sitrus Quick Feet Zigzagoon form the back-line setup mode: Rage Powder or Spore can buy Belly Drum, then Extreme Speed supplies pressure. Allen weaponizes three true first-stage Pokémon and one young mascot through real doubles roles: Light Ball Pikachu, Guts Taillow, Eviolite redirection Paras, and Belly Drum Zigzagoon. Leading with offense keeps the later Rage Powder setup from repeating Calvin's opening redirection pattern. Wally's current Mauville redirection-plus-Belly Drum module is explicitly flagged for replacement when that encounter is audited.

**How it behaves:** Allen uses normal foe-aware doubles scoring plus partner awareness and contextual speed control. The AI can choose immediate Pikachu and Taillow pressure before the later redirection option appears; Rage Powder, Spore, Belly Drum, Fake Out, Electroweb, Protect, and attacks are evaluated normally, with no forced move, target, turn, or switch.

**Why it is hard:** 4 fully authored Pokémon, average BST 278.8, average cap offset +0.5, ace offset +1, and 100% held-item coverage.

**How unique it is:** Closest unrelated roster: Benjamin (17% species overlap). Its species appear across an average of 1.5 unrelated trainer families.

**Counterplay:** The opening pair is vulnerable to Ground, Rock, Intimidate, and coordinated targeting; Protect can also expose Fake Out or consume Taillow's first Guts turn. When the back line appears, Fake Out, Taunt, spread damage, early Grass or Overcoat Pokémon, Hatenna's Magic Bounce, Fire or Flying pressure, or a double target can remove the frail Eviolite Paras before it buys a free Drum. Dreepy, Rotom, and other Ghosts ignore Extreme Speed and Facade, while Intimidate and burns hinder Zigzagoon. The player can disrupt either wave without predicting a forced opening.

**Manual closure:** Battle 4 is difficult because either two-Pokémon wave can snowball, but neither begins behind guaranteed redirection and every enabling action has several legal interruptions. It now demonstrates the intended progression rule directly: young Pokémon can execute expert doubles without being replaced by premature evolved forms.

## 011. May — Route 104 | Rustboro City

**Required Branch · Double · Cap 14 · Extreme 90/100 · Uniqueness 36/100**

**Theme:** Fake Out tempo + active speed control + pivot control

Focus Sash Forecast Castform manually announces the branch's weather. The runtime-generated level-22 Eviolite middle starter is always the same-generation elemental counter to the player's chosen starter: Fire receives sun plus Fire Pledge/Heat Wave/Flare Blitz, Water receives rain plus Water Pledge/Icy Wind/Waterfall, and Grass receives sun plus Grass Pledge/Solar Beam/Seed Bomb. Life Orb Sneasel supplies Fake Out, Feint, Knock Off, and Ice Punch; Sitrus Rotom burns into Hex and pivots with Volt Switch. The rival plans for one starter branch, not the player's whole six. This is Verdant's only dynamic 21-starter forecast battle. Castform, Sneasel, and Rotom do not appear in Battles 1-27; the starter family is the deliberate narrative continuation of Battle 1 rather than incidental reuse. Manual branch weather differs from prior automatic weather speed cores and uses no Mega.

**How it behaves:** All six source records use identical guarded-double, smart-switching, partner, field, and speed-control flags. Existing weather logic values Sun beside Fire or Solar Beam and Rain beside Water; Icy Wind, Forecast, Weather Ball, Fake Out, Feint, Volt Switch, burn, Hex, Eviolite, and Protect remain native. A runtime hook replaces only party slot 1 with the audited middle evolution of the same-generation counter-starter and never mutates player starter state.

**Why it is hard:** 4 fully authored Pokémon, average BST 438.8, average cap offset +1.5, ace offset +2, and 100% held-item coverage.

**How unique it is:** Closest unrelated roster: Brendan (100% species overlap). Its species appear across an average of 4.5 unrelated trainer families.

**Counterplay:** Fake Out, Taunt, sleep, focus fire, immediate weather replacement, Cloud Nine, Air Lock, Protect, or removing Castform's Sash can break the forecast. Knock Off removes Eviolite; status, speed reversal, screens, typed resistances, and focus fire answer every middle starter. Sneasel is fragile and takes Life Orb recoil. Dark, Ghost, Mold Breaker Ground pressure, status prevention, and denying burn reduce Rotom's Hex line. The player can win through the rest of the party rather than one exact starter response.

**Manual closure:** Battle 28 is 10/10 because all 21 starter choices receive a legal, understandable middle-stage continuation while the three shared companions make the fight about the whole team. Levels 21-22, four distinct items, branch-safe native AI, truthful dialogue, and broad weather, item, status, speed, type, and focus-fire counterplay make the optional rival 9.0/10 without overfitting one starter.

## 017. Ivan — Route 104

**Optional · Single · Cap 14 · Extreme 89/100 · Uniqueness 82/100**

**Theme:** Sash Endeavor lure + Schooling HP threshold + Water pressure

Ivan is a single-battle pacing break built as lure, sinker, hook, and school. Focus Sash Luvdisc invites an apparent easy knockout, then trades HP with Endeavor or releases into a counter through Flip Turn. Stunfisk is immune to the obvious Electric answer and can punish contact with Static while attacking both defenses and using Pain Split. Eviolite Tentacool resists the obvious Grass answer and returns Poison, Ice, Water, or Grass coverage. Level-20 Assault Vest Wishiwashi finally forms its 620-BST School, but loses that form as soon as it falls to one-quarter HP. This is Verdant's only fishing-cast singles sequence and first Schooling threshold puzzle. Luvdisc, Stunfisk, Tentacool, and Wishiwashi do not appear in Battles 1-14. It deliberately follows a doubles recital with a talk-only single and uses no rain, speed-control move, setup, hazard, trap, Perish timer, screen, redirection, detonation, item theft, dance, Choice lock, or repeated Water Spout/Shell Smash module. Dondozo and Tatsugiri remain available for a later native Commander double.

**How it behaves:** Ivan remains a native singles trainer with universal foe awareness, viability and faint checks, smart switching, and HP-aware scoring. Existing damage estimation understands Endeavor's current-HP damage, discourages it while Luvdisc has more HP, and values it below half HP; native switching can catch an Electric attack with Stunfisk or a Grass attack with Tentacool. Schooling's level-20 and one-quarter-HP transitions are native. No trainer-only move, target, switch, or turn script is added.

**Why it is hard:** 4 fully authored Pokémon, average BST 341.5, average cap offset +3.25, ace offset +6, and 100% held-item coverage.

**How unique it is:** Closest unrelated roster: Cory (20% species overlap). Its species appear across an average of 5.2 unrelated trainer families.

**Counterplay:** Priority, Ghost immunity, Taunt, multihit attacks, or preserving a low-HP target answer the Sash-Endeavor lure. Water, Grass, Ice, strong special damage, noncontact attacks, and recovery answer Stunfisk; Ground, Psychic, Electric, and strong physical damage answer Tentacool despite Eviolite. Wishiwashi can be burned, intimidated, walled on either attacking side, hit with fixed damage or priority, or deliberately pushed below its visible one-quarter Schooling threshold. Smart switching means one Electric or Grass move is useful but never an automatic sweep; no exact catch, starter, or turn sequence is required.

**Manual closure:** Battle 15 is 10/10 because every member embodies a different part of Ivan's fishing metaphor and every obvious counter is useful without sweeping the roster. Three stage-valid catches at levels 16-17 establish the bait, then a level-20 Schooling ace creates a severe but transparent HP-threshold finish. Four perfect spreads, distinct items, modern-legal moves, adaptive singles AI, and broad type, tempo, contact, status, priority, and threshold counterplay make it an 8.9/10 optional puzzle.

## 078. Huey — Route 109

**Optional · Single · Cap 30 · Extreme 86/100 · Uniqueness 70/100**

**Theme:** Earthquake immunity + rain engine

Wacan Drizzle Pelipper opens with rain-accurate Hurricane, Hydro Pump, Ice Beam, or Roost. Choice Band Tough Claws Perrserker then commits visibly to Iron Head, Close Combat, U-turn, or Play Rough. Assault Vest Steelworker Dhelmise closes through Power Whip, Poltergeist, Anchor Shot, and Earthquake; Anchor Shot can prevent one careless escape. The three are a thematic harbor sequence, not a hidden combo. This is Verdant's first Steelworker Dhelmise and first explicit harbor-anchor singles team. Pelipper, Perrserker, and Dhelmise do not appear in Battles 1-36. It uses no setup move, priority move, active speed control, Protect, terrain, room, partner mechanic, Mega, or custom AI; rain reappears only as a native opener after an eight-battle gap.

**How it behaves:** Huey remains an intentional single with native smart-switching and HP-aware scoring. Drizzle, Wacan Berry, weather accuracy, Roost, Choice lock, Tough Claws, U-turn, Assault Vest, Steelworker, Poltergeist item checks, and Anchor Shot trapping are existing mechanics. No weather script, forced switch, custom selector, or Mega is added.

**Why it is hard:** 3 fully authored Pokémon, average BST 469.0, average cap offset +2.0, ace offset +3, and 100% held-item coverage.

**How unique it is:** Closest unrelated roster: Matt (29% species overlap). Its species appear across an average of 7.0 unrelated trainer families.

**Counterplay:** Weather replacement, Cloud Nine, Air Lock, Electric or Rock pressure, Taunt, and exploiting Roost limit Pelipper. Protect, immunities, resistances, item removal, and switching exploit Perrserker's Choice lock. Fire, Ghost, Dark, Flying, Ice, status, burn, strong special attacks, and removing Assault Vest answer Dhelmise; Anchor Shot must connect before trapping matters. No one port member covers every other weakness.

**Strongest part:** Dhelmise is a memorable post-badge rare encounter and Anchor Shot makes the sailor theme mechanically real without needing special scripting.

**Weakest link:** The members share a port theme more than a competitive engine. That is accepted route pacing: Choice lock, common typed weaknesses, and only one trap make the battle hard but easy to read.

**Manual closure:** Battle 37 is closed at an editorial 8.6/10: three legal levels 31-33, distinct items and unused species, three full-set donors, native singles routing and dialogue, author self-check, and no custom AI. Runtime playtesting remains required before 8.6 is observed.
